title: Voxel Grammar Structure
description: Standalone grammar catalog for grid-based spatial composition. Each element includes meaning, use, and design thinking guidance.

coverage.scope: All elements in this grammar set

thinking_framework.name: Local to Global
thinking_framework.meaning: Small local rules generate larger spatial behavior.
thinking_framework.how_to_use: Compose maps from modules, then evaluate whole-path flow.
thinking_framework.how_to_think: Do not optimize single tiles first; optimize transitions between modules.

thinking_framework.name: Figure and Ground
thinking_framework.meaning: Solid and void are equally authored.
thinking_framework.how_to_use: Alternate built cells with strategic emptiness.
thinking_framework.how_to_think: Treat absence as a constructive material.

thinking_framework.name: Compression and Release
thinking_framework.meaning: Narrow to wide transitions create rhythm and orientation.
thinking_framework.how_to_think: Path drama comes from contrast, not constant width.

thinking_framework.name: Symmetry and Error
thinking_framework.meaning: Order becomes memorable when one deviation is intentional.
thinking_framework.how_to_use: Mirror modules and alter one cell.
thinking_framework.how_to_think: Asymmetry is a signal, not noise.

thinking_framework.name: Threshold Literacy
thinking_framework.meaning: Doors, gates, and vestibules are cognitive markers.
thinking_framework.how_to_use: Separate zones with explicit threshold pieces.
thinking_framework.how_to_think: A threshold should communicate state change.

thinking_framework.name: Topology Awareness
thinking_framework.meaning: Portals and wraps alter adjacency beyond Euclidean layout.
thinking_framework.how_to_use: Attach logic hooks to specific cells, not entire maps.
thinking_framework.how_to_think: Topology is a gameplay rule, not decoration.

compositional_axiom.question: Are larger structures built from more basic grammar?
compositional_axiom.answer: Yes. Composite structures are authored as layered combinations of primitives, operators, and spatial roles.
compositional_axiom.formula: primitives + operators + roles -> modules -> composite structure
compositional_axiom.design_note: Treat named architectures as recipes over a finite base alphabet.

elements.name: Floor
elements.meaning: Default walkable surface.
how_to_use: Use as baseline in all modules.
Keep large regions floor-only for orientation resets.
how_to_think: Floor is neutral context, not an event.
Too much variation removes readability.

elements.name: Void
elements.meaning: Absence of floor; negative space that creates edge conditions.
how_to_use: Carve pits, wells, and reveal chambers.
Pair with rails, walls, or thresholds for safety legibility.
how_to_think: Void is structure by subtraction.
Depth can focus attention more than height.

elements.name: Platform
elements.meaning: Raised walkable tile.
how_to_use: Use for emphasis and line-of-sight control.
Group platforms into plinths and decks.
how_to_think: Height means hierarchy.
Raise only what should be noticed.

elements.name: Pillar
elements.meaning: Vertical accent and obstacle anchor.
how_to_use: Use in pairs for gates.
Use in rows for colonnades.
how_to_think: Pillars are rhythm markers.
Single pillars imply orientation pivots.

elements.name: Wall
elements.meaning: Linear barrier that channels movement.
how_to_use: Build corridors and court perimeters.
Interrupt long walls with apertures.
how_to_think: Wall controls route, not only blockage.
Long uninterrupted walls flatten pacing.

elements.name: Gate
elements.meaning: Passage framed by two supports.
how_to_use: Use between zones with distinct rule sets.
Combine with signage or lighting for clarity.
how_to_think: A gate marks permission.
Gates should read before they are reached.

elements.name: Plinth
elements.meaning: Low 2x2 platform for focal placement.
how_to_use: Place artifacts at center of view cones.
Use as a stable visual anchor in open courts.
how_to_think: Plinth equals significance.
Do not overuse or emphasis collapses.

elements.name: Ramp
elements.meaning: Gradual transition between elevations.
how_to_use: Connect platform heights while preserving flow.
Use with corridor turns for kinetic pacing.
how_to_think: Ramps are verbs in space.
Vertical movement should feel intentional, not abrupt.

elements.name: Place
elements.meaning: Insert a primitive or module at coordinates.
how_to_use: Start from floor field, then place constraints.
Use consistent grid offsets for repeatability.
how_to_think: Placement defines intent.
Every cell should answer why it exists.

elements.name: Repeat
elements.meaning: Copy a module along an axis with spacing.
how_to_use: Create rhythms like colonnades and striped walls.
Use beat intervals to place landmarks.
how_to_think: Repetition creates expectation.
Break expectation once to signal transition.

elements.name: Rotate
elements.meaning: Turn module orientation by 90-degree increments.
how_to_use: Reuse one authored module in four directions.
Compose rotational quartets around center cells.
how_to_think: Rotation preserves identity while changing affordance.
Directionality is part of module meaning.

elements.name: Mirror
elements.meaning: Reflect module across x or z axis.
how_to_use: Generate balanced pairs quickly.
Use mirror-with-error for subtle tension.
how_to_think: Mirrors stabilize orientation.
Perfect symmetry is calm; broken symmetry is narrative.

elements.name: Translate
elements.meaning: Shift a module without changing form.
how_to_use: Build staggered corridors and phase-shifted repeats.
Offset duplicates by one cell for chicanes.
how_to_think: Translation is a relation, not a shape.
Offset controls alignment tension.

sample.effect: module copied one cell to the east

elements.name: Stack Height
elements.meaning: Increase vertical level values to build hierarchy.
how_to_use: Raise landmarks and observation points.
Use stepped stacks for staircase motifs.
how_to_think: Height communicates priority.
Vertical contrast should support route readability.

elements.name: Carve Void
elements.meaning: Subtract occupied cells to create apertures or wells.
how_to_use: Cut doorways, window slits, and anti-columns.
Use carve operations to make thresholds legible.
how_to_think: Subtraction is equivalent to construction.
A carved void should still imply intentional form.

elements.name: Split
elements.meaning: Divide a space into two related subspaces.
how_to_use: Use thin walls or colonnades to split courts.
Assign each half a distinct interaction mode.
how_to_think: Split introduces comparison.
Division can clarify contrast better than separate rooms.

elements.name: Merge
elements.meaning: Combine adjacent modules into one coherent field.
how_to_use: Merge vestibule and court into one flow chain.
Unify materials/heights at join seams.
how_to_think: Merge resolves boundary noise.
A merge should remove ambiguity, not detail.

elements.name: Slip / Shear
elements.meaning: Offset repeated lines to create staggered tension.
how_to_use: Apply to parallel walls for dynamic corridors.
Use with beat gates for syncopated pacing.
how_to_think: Shear is controlled misalignment.
Small offsets can produce large perceptual effects.

elements.name: Phase Shift
elements.meaning: Change repeat parity to alter alignment and rhythm.
how_to_use: Shift every second module by one cell.
Use in wave corridors and field textures.
how_to_think: Phase is a temporal idea applied spatially.
Parity changes can mark zone boundaries.

elements.name: Portal Link
elements.meaning: Declare non-local adjacency between distant cells.
how_to_use: Use for non-Euclid wraps and loop corridors.
Pair with clear frame geometry for user legibility.
how_to_think: Portal links modify topology, not geometry.
Player trust requires consistent portal rules.

elements.name: Center
elements.meaning: Focal cell cluster for primary attention.
how_to_use: Place plinths, key artifacts, or anchor cells.
Use ring courts to reinforce centrality.
how_to_think: Center answers what matters.
A weak center makes the map feel undecided.

elements.name: Edge
elements.meaning: Boundary region where containment is read.
how_to_use: Line with walls, pillars, or colonnades.
Use edge rhythm to drive orientation.
how_to_think: Edges are memory rails.
Consistent edge language reduces disorientation.

elements.name: Corner
elements.meaning: Turning or anchoring condition at boundary intersections.
how_to_use: Place buttress nodes at external corners.
Use inside corners for pockets and reveals.
how_to_think: Corners accumulate directional meaning.
Corner treatment determines whether space feels open or tight.

elements.name: Threshold
elements.meaning: Transition cell set between two states.
how_to_use: Use doorway cuts, gates, and vestibules.
Attach labels or utility markers for explicit transition.
how_to_think: Thresholds are cognitive punctuation.
A good threshold clarifies before crossing.

elements.name: Corridor
elements.meaning: Directed path channel between zones.
how_to_use: Use dogleg, S-bend, and chicane variants for pacing.
Alternate narrow and wide sections for compression/release.
how_to_think: Corridor defines time through space.
Route complexity should serve learning, not confusion.

elements.name: Node
elements.meaning: Decision point where multiple paths meet.
how_to_use: Use T and cross junction modules.
Place annotations at nodes to explain branch choices.
how_to_think: Node quality controls map legibility.
Nodes should expose options without overload.

elements.name: Buffer
elements.meaning: Intermediary chamber easing transition between scales or rules.
how_to_use: Insert vestibules before large courts.
Use small neutral cells to reset orientation.
how_to_think: Buffers prevent abrupt cognitive jumps.
A map without buffers feels brittle.

elements.name: Court
elements.meaning: Open central field enclosed or framed by boundaries.
how_to_use: Use perimeter and split variants for comparison.
Place center artifacts in courts with controlled entries.
how_to_think: Courts are interaction stages.
Court boundaries define audience and focus.

elements.name: T-Junction Wall
elements.meaning: Branch node where one wall joins another mid-span.
how_to_use: Use as branch decision point.
Place signage where branch semantics differ.
how_to_think: T-junction is a controlled fork.
Branches should represent meaningful alternatives.

elements.name: Cross-Junction Wall
elements.meaning: Four-way node with maximal route connectivity.
how_to_use: Use in hub-like intersections.
Reduce clutter near cross-junctions for readability.
how_to_think: Cross-junctions accelerate decision load.
Pair with landmarks to prevent disorientation.

elements.name: Doorway Cut
elements.meaning: Carved opening in an otherwise solid wall.
how_to_use: Place as explicit transition marker.
Use repeated doorway rhythm to signal sequence progression.
how_to_think: A doorway is both permission and direction.
Openings should align with intended view corridors.

elements.name: Window Slit
elements.meaning: Visual aperture without full pass-through.
how_to_use: Preview next zone without granting access.
Use to frame focal artifacts at distance.
how_to_think: Slits create anticipation.
Visibility can precede navigability.

elements.name: Pier Gate
elements.meaning: Two pillars framing a one-cell pass.
how_to_use: Use as lightweight threshold where full wall is too heavy.
Repeat as arcades for temporal rhythm.
how_to_think: Frames can be softer than walls.
Gate cadence can encode progression tempo.

elements.name: Buttress Node
elements.meaning: Wall corner with structural accent pillar.
how_to_use: Use to emphasize turns and outer boundaries.
Use at corners where route should feel fortified.
how_to_think: Buttress implies load and seriousness.
Corner accents can mark sequence phase changes.

elements.name: Dogleg Corridor
elements.meaning: Single right-angle bend with lead-in.
how_to_use: Use to hide direct line-of-sight to target room.
Insert before reveal spaces for pacing.
how_to_think: Dogleg equals deferred information.
Turns can create narrative beats.

elements.name: S-Bend Corridor
elements.meaning: Two opposing turns that modulate flow.
how_to_use: Use for measured traversal between dense nodes.
Pair with rhythmic lighting or labels.
how_to_think: S-bends prevent straight-line autopilot.
Alternating direction keeps attention active.

elements.name: Chicane Corridor
elements.meaning: Offset obstacles forcing zig-zag traversal.
how_to_use: Use to slow movement before key interaction zones.
Combine with pillar rhythm for stronger effect.
how_to_think: Chicane is embodied parsing.
The body learns the rule by navigating it.

elements.name: Vestibule
elements.meaning: Small interstitial chamber between spaces.
how_to_use: Use as a decompression stage.
Use to prepare users for rule/context changes.
how_to_think: Vestibules reduce abruptness.
Buffers are pedagogical, not decorative.

elements.name: Pocket Court
elements.meaning: Small side court attached to a route.
how_to_use: Place optional interactions or side notes here.
Use as quiet zone off major corridors.
how_to_think: Pockets hold secondary meaning.
Not every space needs to be on mainline progression.

elements.name: Perimeter Court
elements.meaning: Ring enclosure with central open field.
how_to_use: Use for central demonstrations or boss-like nodes.
Connect by multiple gates for nonlinear traversal.
how_to_think: Ring form emphasizes center and circulation.
Perimeter is audience, center is performance.

elements.name: Split Court
elements.meaning: Court divided by a thin linear separator.
how_to_use: Stage side-by-side comparisons.
Separate two interaction logics in one room.
how_to_think: Split form means dialogue.
Difference can coexist without full isolation.

elements.name: Plinth Field
elements.meaning: One or more low platforms used as semantic anchors.
how_to_use: Use isolated plinths in open courts.
Assign one concept per plinth cluster.
how_to_think: Plinth = declaration of importance.
Spacing between plinths sets conceptual distance.

elements.name: Dais + Back Wall
elements.meaning: Stage-like composition with backdrop.
how_to_use: Frame explanations or key demonstrations.
Use in sequence finales to increase closure.
how_to_think: Dais configures audience attention.
Backdrop converts platform into statement.

elements.name: Colonnade Strip
elements.meaning: Alternating pillar-void rhythm on boundary lines.
how_to_use: Use as pacing rail along long walks.
Use as visual metronome for progression maps.
how_to_think: Repetition structures memory.
Rhythm can replace signage in familiar sections.

elements.name: Mirror-With-Error
elements.meaning: Near-symmetry with one intentional mismatch.
how_to_use: Highlight one important anomaly.
Use in puzzle teaching around invariants.
how_to_think: Error introduces narrative in otherwise stable systems.
The smallest asymmetry can carry the largest semantic weight.

elements.name: Hollow Wall
elements.meaning: Thick shell wall with interior pass-through.
how_to_use: Hide traversal channels in apparent barriers.
Use as advanced legibility challenge.
how_to_think: Surface appearance and traversal truth can diverge.
Hollow structures reward exploration.

elements.name: Void Pillar
elements.meaning: Column-shaped vertical subtraction (anti-column).
how_to_use: Mark key centers with absence instead of mass.
Use as contrast against physical pillar sets.
how_to_think: Negative landmarks can guide as strongly as positive ones.
Void pillars expose figure-ground reversibility.

elements.name: Non-Euclid Wrap Corridor
elements.meaning: Straight corridor with portal-linked wrap adjacency.
how_to_use: Use sparingly to teach topology shifts.
Always signal wrap behavior with clear framing.
how_to_think: Euclidean geometry can remain while topology changes.
Consistency of rule is more important than realism.

elements.name: Loop Portal Pair
elements.meaning: Two portals forming a circulation cycle.
how_to_use: Create repeatable loops for training or rhythm.
Use loop exits to branch into optional side content.
how_to_think: Loops create temporal structures in map traversal.
Repeated path can support mastery or disorientation.

elements.name: Anchor Cell
elements.meaning: Reference cell that reorients local coordinate reading.
how_to_use: Use at major node entries and topology transitions.
Bind HUD/text annotations to anchor location.
how_to_think: Anchor cells reduce cognitive drift in complex maps.
Orientation cues are part of grammar, not post-processing.

elements.name: Japanese Garden (Mini)
elements.meaning: Asymmetric contemplative micro-court with stones, stepping path, and framed entry.
how_to_use: Use as a calm pocket between dense algorithm spaces.
Place one focused artifact at edge rather than center.
how_to_think: Asymmetry should feel intentional, not random.
Negative space and path cadence are the main content.

assembly_steps: Lay a quiet 7x7 floor field.
Place offset stone nodes (pillars/platforms) asymmetrically.
Carve selective void pockets for rake-like contrast.
Add one gate/threshold for controlled entry.

elements.name: Templar Compound (Mini)
elements.meaning: Compact fortified court with axial gate and cross-ordered interior.
how_to_use: Use for high-clarity, high-discipline spaces in sequence transitions.
Place rule-heavy demonstrations inside this structure.
how_to_think: Axial symmetry communicates doctrine and control.
Use one deliberate break if you want narrative tension.

assembly_steps: Build a square perimeter wall.
Insert one central gate on primary axis.
Lay a cross-axis interior path.
Raise a small central platform as focus.

elements.name: Amphitheatre (Mini)
elements.meaning: Tiered semi-circular seating condition facing a stage platform.
how_to_use: Use for collective viewing of dynamic artifacts.
Align stage with strongest entry axis.
how_to_think: Height tiers encode audience hierarchy and sightline logic.
Amp spaces are about orientation convergence.

assembly_steps: Create a stage strip at one edge.
Stack stepped tiers opposite the stage.
Keep a central aisle or split lane for access.
Frame lateral edges with low walls.

elements.name: Mini Fortress
elements.meaning: Small defensive enclosure with corner towers and controlled gate.
how_to_use: Use as challenge node around hazards or enemies.
Place one protected objective inside.
how_to_think: Fortress grammar emphasizes chokepoints and visibility control.
Corner towers should support surveillance logic.

assembly_steps: Lay a square wall ring with one gate break.
Raise corner towers with higher pillar values.
Optionally carve moat-like void outside one face.
Reserve interior as protected court.

elements.name: Torii Threshold (Mini)
elements.meaning: Symbolic framed gate for ritualized entry into a distinct zone.
how_to_use: Place at entry to contemplative or sacred subspaces.
Use repeated torii frames for processional paths.
how_to_think: The frame changes interpretation of the next cells.
Threshold semantics can be cultural, not purely functional.

assembly_steps: Place two supports with one-cell pass.
Add top lintel marker via elevated accents if desired.
Align with processional path.

elements.name: Bastion Ring (Mini)
elements.meaning: Polygonal-like defensive ring approximated on grid with offset bastions.
how_to_use: Use when you want fortress feel with non-rectangular rhythm.
Pair with loop corridors or patrol routes.
how_to_think: Bastions are geometry for lateral visibility.
Offset projections encode directional control.

assembly_steps: Start from perimeter court.
Shear selected edge segments outward as bastions.
Merge ring and projections into one path network.

elements.name: Pyramid Terrace (Mini)
elements.meaning: Stepped concentric mass rising from broad base to focused apex.
how_to_use: Use as a hierarchy landmark: base for circulation, apex for key artifact.
Place at sequence pivots where you want clear progression from edge to center.
how_to_think: Pyramid principle is compression: many routes at base, one point at top.
Each step is both boundary and platform, so vertical order becomes legible.

assembly_steps: Lay a square base footprint.
Step inward each ring while increasing height.
Reserve one apex cell as focal node.
Optionally cut one processional entry axis.

elements.name: Half Pyramid Section
elements.meaning: A pyramid cut by a plane, exposing stepped interior profile.
how_to_use: Use to teach structure logic by showing inside and outside simultaneously.
Place a path along the cut face so players read each terrace as a chapter.
how_to_think: Half-pyramid principle is revelation: sectioning turns hidden order into pedagogy.
One half remains mass, the other half becomes void/interface.

assembly_steps: Author a full stepped pyramid block.
Split along one axis.
Carve one half to expose the stepped section.
Add a ramp/corridor on the section face for readable traversal.
